name: Create Administrator
description:
The User Administrator is the first user you should create. This user will have rights to create other users and grant any privileges on the database.

1. START the MondoDB service if it is not running:

[root@centos ~]# service mongod start
Starting mongod:                                           [  OK  ]

2. Connect to the service from localhost (ie. the same machine that MongoDB is running on):

[root@centos mongo]# mongo
MongoDB shell version: 3.0.1
connecting to: test
Server has startup warnings: 
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] 
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] ** WARNING: /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled is 'always'.
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] **        We suggest setting it to 'never'
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] 
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] ** WARNING: /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag is 'always'.
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] **        We suggest setting it to 'never'
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] 
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] ** WARNING: soft rlimits too low. rlimits set to 1024 processes, 64000 files. Number of processes should be at least 32000 : 0.5 times number of files.
2015-03-31T18:03:00.446+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] 
>

Note that by default you are connected to the test database.

3. Switch to the admin database.



> use admin
switched to db admin
>

The use command will switch to the database you specify, creating it if it doesn't exist. The admin database will hold your admin user(s).

4. Create the administrator user

We use the db.createUser command to create a new user. We will grant the administrator "userAdminAnyDatabase" rights, which means the user can create USERS and GRANT ROLES to any user on the system. We will use the username "siteUserAdmin" and assign the password "password".

Copy and paste this text into the mongo shell:

db.createUser(
  {
    user: "siteUserAdmin",
    pwd: "password",
    roles: [ { role: "userAdminAnyDatabase", db: "admin" } ]
  }
)

The output will look like this:

> db.createUser(
...   {
...     user: "siteUserAdmin",
...     pwd: "password",
...     roles: [ { role: "userAdminAnyDatabase", db: "admin" } ]
...   }
... )
Successfully added user: {
    "user" : "siteUserAdmin",
    "roles" : [
        {
            "role" : "userAdminAnyDatabase",
            "db" : "admin"
        }
    ]
}
>

5. Enable authentication

Now that the admin user has been created, you should enable authentication on the system. Exit the mongo shell and edit the /etc/mongod.conf file: 
> exit
bye
[root@centos mongo]# vi /etc/mongod.conf

Change the following from

# Turn on/off security.  Off is currently the default
#noauth=true
#auth=true

to

# Turn on/off security.  Off is currently the default
#noauth=true
auth=true

Restart the MongoDB instance:

[root@centos mongo]# service mongod restart
Stopping mongod:                                           [  OK  ]
Starting mongod:                                           [  OK  ]
[root@centos mongo]#

Now, only authenticated users will be allowed to browse or modify the databases.

6. Test that authentication works

Create a new database, and then try to run a query on it:

[root@centos mongo]# mongo
MongoDB shell version: 3.0.1
connecting to: test
> use mynewdb
switched to db mynewdb
> db.stuff.find()
Error: error: { "$err" : "not authorized for query on mynewdb.stuff", "code" : 13 }
>

7. Authenticate as the "siteUserAdmin" user and try again:

> use admin
switched to db admin
> db.auth("siteUserAdmin", "password")
1
> use mynewdb
switched to db mynewdb
> db.stuff.find()
Error: error: { "$err" : "not authorized for query on mynewdb.stuff", "code" : 13 }
>

Note that the user still can NOT browse the database. This is because they only have "userAdmin" rights, so they can only administer USERS.

8. Create a user administrator for a SINGLE database

We now create an admin user that can administer a single database, in this case 'mynewdb'

> use mynewdb
switched to db mynewdb
> db.createUser(
... {
...   user: "mynewdbUserAdmin",
...   pwd:  "password",
...   roles: [ { role: "userAdmin", db: "mynewdb" } ]
... }
... )
Successfully added user: {
    "user" : "mynewdbUserAdmin",
    "roles" : [
        {
            "role" : "userAdmin",
            "db" : "mynewdb"
        }
    ]
}
>

We now have a user who can GRANT privileges to users ONLY in the 'mynewdb' database.

name: Create a Database User
description:
Once you have created a User Administrator, you can now create users and grant them privileges so that they can use the database.

Here we assume that you have created the "mynewdbUserAdmin". We will use this user to create a Database User.

1 Authenticate as the User Administrator

Make sure you are still in the database "mynewdb" Authenticate using the db.auth() command:

> db
mynewdb
> db.auth("mynewdbUserAdmin", "password")
1
>

The '1' output shows that the authentication was successful.

2 Create a user in this database.

Call the db.createUser() command:

db.createUser(
    {
      user: "mynewdbUser",
      pwd: "password",
      roles: [
     { role: "readWrite", db: "mynewdb" }
      ]
    }
)

You will see the following:

> db.createUser(
...     {
...       user: "mynewdbUser",
...       pwd: "password",
...       roles: [
...          { role: "readWrite", db: "mynewdb" }
...       ]
...     }
... )
Successfully added user: {
    "user" : "mynewdbUser",
    "roles" : [
        {
            "role" : "readWrite",
            "db" : "mynewdb"
        }
    ]
}
>

The new user "mynewdbUser" has READ and WRITE privileges on the "mynewdb" database.

name: Administer Users
description:
1. Get information about a user

You can get information about a user with the db.getUser() command:

> db.getUser("mynewdbUser")
{
    "_id" : "mynewdb.mynewdbUser",
    "user" : "mynewdbUser",
    "db" : "mynewdb",
    "roles" : [
        {
            "role" : "readWrite",
            "db" : "mynewdb"
        }
    ]
}
>

Here you see the user "mynewdbUser" can read and write to the database "mynewdb".

2. Change a user's password

Changing passwords can be done using the db.changeUserPassword() command:

> db.changeUserPassword("mynewdbUser", "12345678")
>

This will change the password of user "mynewdbUser" to "12345678"

name: Recovering the Administrator password
description:
If you lose the administrator password, you can reset it if you have root access to the MongoDB machine.

1. Disable MongoDB authentication

Change the configuration file "code>/etc/mongod.conf" so that "noauth" and "auth" are commented out:

[root@centos ~]# vi /etc/mongod.conf
...
# Turn on/off security.  Off is currently the default
#noauth=true
#auth=true

2. Restart the "mongod" service

[root@centos mongo]# service mongod restart
Stopping mongod:                                           [  OK  ]
Starting mongod:                                           [  OK  ]
[root@centos mongo]#

3. Change the password

Change the Administrator's password using the db.changeUserPassword() command:

[root@centos mongo]# mongo
MongoDB shell version: 3.0.1
connecting to: test
2015-03-31T19:31:05.072+0200 I CONTROL  [initandlisten] 
> use admin
switched to db admin
> db.getUser("siteUserAdmin")
{
    "_id" : "admin.siteUserAdmin",
    "user" : "siteUserAdmin",
    "db" : "admin",
    "roles" : [
        {
            "role" : "userAdminAnyDatabase",
            "db" : "admin"
        }
    ]
}
> db.changeUserPassword("siteUserAdmin", "87654321")
>

name: Backup and Restore
description:
As of version 2.8, you can only backup and restore databases while the MongoDB instance is running.

1. Backing up the entire database

Backups are created using the mongodump command. The command creates a directory structure matching the databases in the system. You will need to have set aside a location to store the backups.

1.1 Determine where the backup should go, and create a new directory if it doesn't exist

[root@centos mongo]# mkdir -p /backup

1.2 Run the mongodump command to dump the entire database

[root@centos mongo]# mongodump --out /backup/
2015-03-31T21:35:30.553+0200    writing admin.system.users to /backup/admin/system.users.bson
2015-03-31T21:35:30.553+0200    writing admin.system.indexes to /backup/admin/system.indexes.bson
2015-03-31T21:35:30.554+0200    writing admin.system.users metadata to /backup/admin/system.users.metadata.json
2015-03-31T21:35:30.556+0200    done dumping admin.system.users
2015-03-31T21:35:30.556+0200    writing admin.system.version to /backup/admin/system.version.bson
2015-03-31T21:35:30.557+0200    writing admin.system.version metadata to /backup/admin/system.version.metadata.json
2015-03-31T21:35:30.559+0200    done dumping admin.system.version
[root@centos mongo]#

Your backup has been successfully created.

2. Restoring the entire database

As with backing up, this can only be done while MongoDB is running. Restoring will by default MERGE all information in the backup with all current information. This may cause unwanted side-effects. To avoid this, you can DROP all information in the database as you perform the restore. This will ensure that only information in the backup will be in the database after the restore.

2.1 Locate the backup on your system

[root@centos ~]# ls /backup/
admin
[root@centos ~]#

2.2 Run the mongorestore command to MERGE all information in the backup with the current information:

[root@centos backup]# mongorestore /backup
2015-03-31T21:43:38.204+0200    building a list of dbs and collections to restore from /backup/ dir
2015-03-31T21:43:38.205+0200    restoring users from admin/system.users.bson
2015-03-31T21:43:38.210+0200    done
[root@centos backup]#

2.3 Run the mongorestore command to DROP all information in the database before restoring:

[root@centos backup]# mongorestore --drop /backup
2015-03-31T21:44:34.307+0200    building a list of dbs and collections to restore from /backup/ dir
2015-03-31T21:44:34.308+0200    restoring users from admin/system.users.bson
2015-03-31T21:44:34.312+0200    done
[root@centos backup]#

3. Backing up and restoring a specific database

You can use the above two commands to backup or restore individual databases, instead of all databases. Specify the database you want to back up or restore with the --db parameter:

3.1 Backing up a specific database:

[root@centos ~]# mongodump --db admin --out /backup/
2015-03-31T21:53:40.450+0200    writing admin.system.indexes to /backup/admin/system.indexes.bson
2015-03-31T21:53:40.450+0200    writing admin.system.users to /backup/admin/system.users.bson
2015-03-31T21:53:40.451+0200    writing admin.system.version to /backup/admin/system.version.bson
2015-03-31T21:53:40.452+0200    writing admin.system.version metadata to /backup/admin/system.version.metadata.json
2015-03-31T21:53:40.455+0200    writing admin.system.users metadata to /backup/admin/system.users.metadata.json
2015-03-31T21:53:40.457+0200    done dumping admin.system.version
2015-03-31T21:53:40.466+0200    done dumping admin.system.users
[root@centos ~]#

Note this creates a subfolder "admin/" in the "/backup/" location. You will use this to restore the database.

3.2 Restoring a specific database:

[root@centos ~]# mongorestore --db admin /backup/admin/
2015-03-31T21:56:22.270+0200    building a list of collections to restore from /backup/admin/ dir
2015-03-31T21:56:22.271+0200    restoring users from /backup/admin/system.users.bson
2015-03-31T21:56:22.275+0200    done
[root@centos ~]#

Note that you have to specify BOTH the database you want to restore ("admin") as well as the location of the backup of the database ("/backup/admin")

If you get the pathname wrong you will see an error like this:

[root@centos ~]# mongorestore --db admin /backup/
2015-03-31T21:55:47.432+0200    building a list of collections to restore from /backup/ dir
2015-03-31T21:55:47.432+0200    don't know what to do with subdirectory "/backup/admin", skipping...
2015-03-31T21:55:47.432+0200    done
